hints: Focus on the shape of the graph, especially the very large drop between two consecutive elements. What change in electronic structure causes that?
Notice that B is a high peak followed by a sharp fall to C, which is the classic signature of a noble gas followed by a new alkali metal.
Work backwards from B to identify A, then ask which Group forms a simple covalent hydride of formula HX.
walkthrough:
**Spot the big drop**

Think like a detective. First ionisation energy generally rises across a period, then falls sharply when a new shell starts.

Here B to C is a huge fall, so a full shell has just finished and a new one is starting.

**Assign the Groups**

That pattern tells us B must be a Group 18 noble gas with a very stable full shell, and C must be the next Group 1 alkali metal with one easy-to-remove outer electron.

Since atomic numbers are consecutive:
$$ A (Group\ 17) \to B (Group\ 18) \to C (Group\ 1) \to D (Group\ 2) $$

**Use the HX clue**

We need an element X that forms a covalent $HX$ molecule with hydrogen. That means X needs one more electron to complete its shell, so Group 17 halogen.

That is exactly element A, for example $F$ to $Ne$ to $Na$ to $Mg$, where $F$ forms covalent $HF$.

options.A: Correct. A is the element just before the noble gas peak B, so it is a Group 17 halogen. Halogens form covalent hydrides like $HF$, $HCl$ with formula $HX$.
options.B: Not correct. B is the peak with highest first ionisation energy, a Group 18 noble gas such as $Ne$. It is inert and does not form $HX$.
options.C: Not correct. C is just after the big drop, a Group 1 alkali metal such as $Na$. It forms ionic hydride $NaH$, not covalent $HX$, and its formula with H would be $XH$, not $HX$ as the electronegative partner.
options.D: Not correct. D is one after C with slightly higher ionisation energy, a Group 2 metal such as $Mg$. It forms ionic $MgH_2$, not covalent $HX$.
